desc:
Among all non-empty contiguous subarrays of nums, find the ones with the largest sum. Several subarrays can share that largest sum, so pick one canonically: the one with the smallest start index, and if there is still a tie, the one with the smallest end index.

Return the three numbers [sum, start, end], where start and end are 0-based and inclusive.

Examples: [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4] gives [6, 3, 6]. For [1, -1, 1] the largest sum is 1, reached by [0,0], [0,2] and [2,2]; the answer is [1, 0, 0].
hints: First compute only the best sum: let cur be the best sum of a subarray ending at the current index. Should the previous run be extended, or should a new run start here?
A previous run is worth extending when its sum is not negative. Remember the start index of the current run alongside cur.
Update the global answer when cur is larger, or when it is equal and (start, end) is lexicographically smaller. When the previous run sums to exactly 0, keep extending: that keeps the earlier start.
editorial: This is Kadane's algorithm with bookkeeping. For every index i, keep the best sum cur of a subarray ending at i and the smallest start s that achieves it. If the run before i has sum < 0, it only hurts, so restart at i. Otherwise extend it. When the earlier run has sum exactly 0, extending gives the same total as restarting but with a smaller start, which is what the tie rule wants.

Any subarray with the globally largest sum must also be the best subarray ending at its own last index (otherwise a better subarray would exist), so looking at the best candidate per end index loses nothing. Compare candidates by (sum desc, start asc, end asc). One pass, O(n) time and O(1) space.
